title: A wall to divide them
saying: mūrumque per octōgintā mīlia passuum prīmus dūxit, quī barbarōs Rōmānōsque dīvideret
author: Historia Augusta

edition.name: Historia Augusta, Latin text of the Loeb Classical Library edition (D. Magie), as presented on LacusCurtius (Bill Thayer), whose Latin pages credit "a Loeb Classical Library" edition of MCMXXI (1921); public domain

source_text: Ergo conversis regio more militibus Britanniam petiit, in qua multa correxit murumque per octoginta milia passuum primus duxit, qui barbaros Romanosque divideret.
excerpt_note: Section 11.2 complete, one sentence. The edition's footnote on regio (an apparatus note listing conjectures) is not reproduced.

translation: So, having reformed the soldiers in kingly fashion, he made for Britain, where he set many things right and was the first to build a wall, eighty miles long, to divide the barbarians and the Romans.
translation_note: conversīs ... mīlitibus is an ablative absolute, looking back to the military reforms of chapter 10. The reading rēgiō mōre is doubted: the edition's apparatus lists the conjectures egregio (Novak), rigido (Frankfurter) and recto (Baehrens). per octōgintā mīlia passuum is extent of space; quī ... dīvideret is a relative clause of purpose ("a wall to divide").

essay.t: As Historic England's guide to linear frontiers points out, this is the only classical literary statement of what Hadrian's Wall was for; other passages, such as the Life of Severus (18.2), credit Severus with a wall across the island.

It comes from the Life of Hadrian in the Historia Augusta, a collection that claims six authors writing around AD 300 but which Hermann Dessau argued in 1889, in a view now generally accepted, was the work of one author writing toward the end of the fourth century or later.
Where its claims can be tested, the Last Historians of Rome project warns, they have often proved unfounded, so anything not corroborated elsewhere is under suspicion.
Here, unusually, the physical evidence supports the core of the claim.

English Heritage dates the start of building to AD 122 and gives the length as 73 miles, which is 80 Roman miles, from Wallsend on the Tyne to Bowness-on-Solway: the text's octoginta milia passuum fits.
Britannica says Hadrian visited Britain in 122; English Heritage says the Wall was built mainly by soldiers of the province's three legions and took at least six years.
Historic England adds that work continued into the 130s and that forts were added part-way through.

The text says the Wall was to divide barbarians and Romans; English Heritage and Britannica both quote the biographer as saying it was "to separate the Romans from the barbarians", with the order reversed.
Archaeologists do not read it as a simple barrier: English Heritage and Britannica stress control of movement across the frontier.
Historic England sets out a debate between a controlled border, whose gated milecastles may have been used to collect taxes, and a more aggressive military posture once the forts were added.
Doubts remain about the sentence itself: the apparatus of this edition records conjectures for regio, "in kingly fashion", such as egregio and rigido.
The Wall was left for about twenty years while the Antonine Wall further north was in use, reoccupied around AD 160, and served as the frontier for nearly 300 years.
